candidates.headline: A single global flattened coverage threshold does not guarantee the per-query coverage that Equation 3 specifies
candidates.claim: Algorithm 4 ranks all (query-block x key-block) scores in one flattened list and stops when the global sum reaches gamma. Equation 3 and its Appendix A rationale require coverage of at least gamma for every query position. These are different stopping rules, so individual query blocks can be left below gamma.
candidates.paper_fact: In Algorithm 4, we flatten and normalize the estimated attention map, then identify the minimum computational budget required for the sum of scores to exceed a given threshold γ.
candidates.premise: If rows of the pooled map are each softmax-normalized and then jointly renormalized, every row carries equal mass. Selecting the largest entries globally still favors rows with peaked distributions. Rows with flat distributions have small per-entry values and are picked last.
candidates.inference: With a global cutoff, a peaked query block can reach full coverage using few key blocks. A flat query block may get only a fraction of the blocks it needs to reach gamma. This is a different optimization target from the per-query one in Eq. 3.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative arithmetic, NOT a measurement. Two query blocks, four key blocks each, rows already softmaxed. Row A = [0.85, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05]. Row B = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]. After global normalization (divide by 2), A = [0.425, 0.025, 0.025, 0.025] and B = 0.125 each. With gamma = 0.5, the global rule picks A1 (0.425) and one B entry (0.125), which totals 0.55. Row B then has only 25% of its own mass covered, while a per-row rule at 0.5 would need 2 of B's blocks.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If query blocks in a Query-Aware head differ strongly in how peaked their pooled distributions are, flat query blocks receive less coverage than gamma. This could matter more for tasks that need per-position fidelity than for needle-style retrieval.
candidates.critical_link: Ranking by absolute normalized block score across all rows, rather than within each row, decides which query blocks are starved.
necessary_conditions: Query blocks in the head have heterogeneous peakedness.
The cutoff gamma is low enough that the global cumulative sum stops before flat rows are reached.
Floor mechanisms (first/last key blocks, 1024-token minimum) do not already cover the flat rows' needs.
defeaters: The authors report that a per-query-block variant performs comparably on RULER.
The first and last key blocks of each query block are always retained, and each head computes at least 1024 tokens.
Most heads use the Vertical-Slash path, so few heads are affected at tau = 0.1.

candidates.headline: Reaching gamma on the flattened block-pooled attention map does not guarantee gamma coverage for each query row
candidates.claim: Eq. 3 states the coverage constraint per query position (for all i). The Query-Aware implementation (Algorithm 4) flattens the whole block-pooled map and stops once the global sum reaches gamma. That does not ensure each query block's own mass reaches gamma, so the per-row premise of the Appendix A error bound is not enforced by the code path.
candidates.paper_fact: Our sparse attention mechanism aims to select the smallest possible subsets Si for each query position i while ensuring that the sum of normalized attention scores within each subset meets a predefined cumulative attention threshold γ.
candidates.premise: In general, a global cumulative-mass cutoff over a matrix normalized to sum to 1 places no lower bound on the mass captured within any single row. Rows that hold little of the total pooled mass can be left under-covered while rows that hold more are over-covered.
candidates.inference: Algorithm 4 flattens and normalizes the pooled map over all (query block, key block) pairs and takes the top entries until the global sum reaches gamma. Row-level coverage is therefore not guaranteed, and the per-row bound (1 - a_S) * sum|v_j| need not hold for every query block. Block-level mass is also not token-level mass.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: two query blocks with pooled mass 0.8 and 0.2 of the flattened total. With gamma = 0.8, selecting every entry of block 1 satisfies the threshold. Block 2 then has zero selected pooled mass from this step, apart from the forced first/last key blocks and the 1024-token floor.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If attention mass is concentrated in a few query blocks, so that row masses in the pooled map are very uneven, then the flattened threshold can leave low-mass query blocks poorly covered. In that case the per-row error guarantee does not carry over.
candidates.critical_link: The per-row constraint in Eq. 3 and the single global cumulative sum in Algorithm 4 are treated as the same objective. Only the first is what the Appendix A bound assumes.

Keys that earlier queries need get lower scores and may be dropped for all rows. The paper evaluates only RULER and InfiniteBench, so this case is untested.

candidates.claim: Algorithm 4 builds and sorts a pooled block map with (n/b)^2 entries. Appendix G's complexity list gives index construction as O(n log n) and attributes it to the representative attention scores, which is the Vertical-Slash route. The listed complexity therefore does not cover the Query-Aware path, and its extra cost grows quadratically in n/b.

candidates.premise: A pooled map over n/b blocks per side has (n/b)^2 entries, and sorting it costs at least that many operations. This quantity grows quadratically with sequence length. It is not O(n log n) for fixed block size b.
candidates.inference: For heads routed to the Query-Aware path, index construction cost scales with (n/b)^2 rather than n log n. The Appendix G overhead summary and the Figure 6 latency share therefore apply to the mixed head population, not to this path in isolation.

candidates.headline: Failing the pooled-estimate test does not imply a head has Vertical-Slash structure
candidates.claim: A head is routed to the Vertical-Slash path whenever its pooled block-attention estimate diverges from the true distribution by at least τ. That test measures estimate reliability, not whether the head's attention is vertical or diagonal. Heads with diffuse, non-line attention can end up with lines imposed on them.
candidates.paper_fact: Otherwise, the approximation is inadequate, we fall back to a more conservative approach.
candidates.premise: A large Jensen-Shannon distance between pooled and true block attention can come from many causes, such as fine-grained intra-block structure or flat distributions. Only some of these causes produce vertical or slash lines.
candidates.inference: The routing rule is a binary comparison of dJS against τ, with the else branch set to vertical_slash. The paper's Figure 8 finding that most heads use Vertical-Slash is therefore partly a product of the routing rule. It is not independent evidence that those heads have line structure. The paper itself notes Query-Aware heads can also look vertical-slash, so the correspondence between the label and the structure is loose in both directions.
candidates.conditional_consequence: For a head with weak line structure that also fails the pooled test, line selection must meet γ with many lines or lose mass. Either outcome erodes the sparsity or accuracy that the fallback is meant to protect.
candidates.critical_link: The fallback is chosen by estimator failure, with no check that line structure actually explains the head's attention.
necessary_conditions: Some heads fail the pooled test for reasons unrelated to line structure.
Those heads have attention spread beyond a few verticals and slashes.
The head matters for the task output.
defeaters: Most failing heads do have strong sink and local-offset structure, as the paper's Figure 8 suggests.
The γ rule adaptively adds lines to compensate for diffuse heads.
The 1024-token floor protects extremely sparse heads.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that many heads are misrouted; the paper reports no such count.
Do not infer that the pooled test is a poor estimator of attention quality.
Do not infer a specific accuracy loss from this mechanism.

candidates.headline: A minimum-budget floor does not imply a gain at every gamma
candidates.claim: In Table 10 the 1024-token floor gives a large gain at gamma 0.9 but is neutral or negative on average for LLaMA at gamma 0.95. Several long-context cells at 0.95 are worse with the floor. The floor therefore looks like a gamma-coupled rescue mechanism, not a uniform improvement.
candidates.paper_fact: Table 10 demonstrates that when γ is high, the model effectively captures most of the important tokens, making a minimum budget limit unnecessary.
candidates.premise: A per-head token floor only changes the computation for heads whose cumulative-attention selection would otherwise fall below the floor. When gamma is high, fewer heads fall below it.
candidates.inference: Table 10 shows a large floor effect at gamma 0.9 (LLaMA avg 84.78 without floor vs 88.38 with 1024; GLM 85.26 vs 88.58). At gamma 0.95 the effect is small and mixed. LLaMA avg is 89.42 without floor vs 89.18 with 1024, with 32k at 92.31 vs 89.42 and 64k at 85.34 vs 82.93. GLM avg is 88.82 vs 89.34. The Section 4.3 phrase 'enhances performance' is stated without the gamma boundary that Appendix F.5 gives.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: if 2 of 1000 heads need fewer than 1024 tokens to reach gamma, the floor changes 0.2% of heads and the accuracy change is mostly noise. If 150 of 1000 heads need fewer, the floor changes the computation of many heads and can matter.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the floor acts through heads that fall below 1024 tokens, a user who lowers gamma below 0.9 for speed should expect the floor to matter more, not less. This regime is not tested in Table 10, which only covers gamma 0.95 and 0.9.
candidates.critical_link: The inference needs the number of heads under the floor to grow as gamma falls. The paper states this qualitatively but does not report per-head budgets or counts of floored heads.
necessary_conditions: The floor binds on a fraction of heads that grows as gamma decreases.
Per-cell differences of a few points at gamma 0.95 are noise-level, so the sign of the 0.95 effect is uncertain.
defeaters: The 32k and 64k gaps at 0.95 may be sampling variance, as the mechanism notes suggest. The paper does not explain them.
The floor may change which heads are re-ranked, which would add an interaction beyond simple budget increase.
Only two models and one benchmark (RULER) are tested.
do_not_infer: That the floor hurts accuracy at high gamma.
That the floor is useless at gamma 0.95. GLM avg improves from 88.82 to 89.34.
Any behavior for gamma below 0.9, which is not in Table 10.

candidates.headline: Meeting a cumulative attention-mass threshold gamma does not guarantee that a head still works
candidates.claim: The dynamic budget is chosen per head and per prompt as the smallest set whose estimated attention mass reaches gamma. Reaching that mass does not ensure the head's function is preserved. The paper itself needs an extra minimum-budget floor to stop some heads from collapsing at lower gamma.
candidates.paper_fact: Our findings reveal that setting a minimum budget threshold enhances performance and prevents the collapse of attention heads with extremely high sparsity ratios.
candidates.premise: Attention-mass coverage is a proxy for output fidelity. The Appendix A bound, (1 - a_S) * sum|v_j|, is only an upper bound, and it grows with context length. In Algorithm 3, mass is estimated from the last block_size queries, not from every query.
candidates.inference: If mass coverage were sufficient, the minimum-budget floor would not be needed. Because a floor is needed when gamma is small, the mass criterion alone can leave some heads under-provisioned. Gamma therefore bounds estimated coverage, not per-prompt accuracy.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: a head whose attention is concentrated on a few sink tokens reaches 0.9 mass with a handful of tokens. If a retrieval-critical but low-mass key is then dropped, the head's output changes in a way the mass criterion does not register.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If gamma is lowered to gain speed (Table 5 shows 128k speedups rising from 2.43x at 0.95 to 9.81x at 0.6), per-prompt accuracy can fall. The mass criterion gives no warning when this happens.
candidates.critical_link: The estimated mass reaching gamma does not mean the sparse head output stays close to the dense output.
necessary_conditions: gamma is small enough that some heads fall below a workable token count
the selected indices are evaluated against the true attention mass, not the block-pooled or representative-query estimate
no minimum-budget floor is applied

A large minimum budget, plus the first and last key blocks being always kept, may mask the issue in practice
The paper says that at high gamma a floor is unnecessary

Do not infer that the floor is the only guard against collapse
Do not infer that the Appendix A bound is wrong

candidates.headline: A per-model gamma fixed at 0.9 or 0.95 does not imply or guarantee a bounded accuracy loss relative to full attention
candidates.claim: The paper fixes gamma per model (0.9 for Yi and Qwen, 0.95 for LLaMA and GLM) and presents it as a speed-accuracy knob. Gamma only sets a target for retained attention mass. The paper never states an accuracy-loss tolerance that the chosen gamma is meant to satisfy. How the values were selected is not described. Whether they transfer to other models, tasks or lengths is not tested.
candidates.paper_fact: We set γ = 0.9 for Yi-9B-200k and Qwen2-7B-Instruct model, and 0.95 for the other models.
candidates.premise: A cumulative-attention-mass threshold is a proxy for output fidelity. The paper's own bound in Appendix A scales as (1 - a_S) times the sum of |v_j| over all L positions, so the same retained mass can allow a larger worst-case error as L grows or as value norms change. How much task-relevant signal sits in the dropped mass depends on the model and the task.
candidates.inference: A gamma that gives near-parity on one model may give a larger loss on another. Table 1 is consistent with this. At gamma 0.9, Yi scores 76.32 against 79.49 for full attention (about 3.2 points lower). GLM at gamma 0.9 is 88.58 against 89.06 (Table 3), and LLaMA at 0.9 is 88.38 against 88.70. Because no loss target is stated, 'near full attention' is not defined by the paper. The values are consistent with having been picked on the reporting benchmark, but the paper does not say how they were picked.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: suppose model P has heads where 0.9 of the mass sits on a few tokens, and model Q has flatter heads where the last 0.1 of the mass is spread over many tokens, some of them task-critical. The same gamma = 0.9 would then drop a few irrelevant tokens in P and many relevant ones in Q.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a new model or task has flatter or more task-critical attention tails than LLaMA, then reusing gamma = 0.9 or 0.95 can cost more accuracy than the Table 5 sweep suggests. The user then has to re-tune gamma.

Task-relevant information lies in the tail of the attention distribution that gamma discards.

candidates.headline: A cumulative-mass threshold gamma does not guarantee a safe per-head budget without an auxiliary minimum-budget rule
candidates.claim: At a lower gamma, heads with very peaked estimated attention can receive a tiny selected set, and the gamma rule alone does not prevent this. The reported results rely on a separate 1024-token floor and forced first/last key blocks, so the observed accuracy reflects gamma coupled with those rules and not gamma alone.
candidates.paper_fact: To ensure that all attention heads work normally, we retain the first and last key blocks of each query block, while also requiring each attention head to compute at least 1024 tokens.
candidates.premise: In general, a mass-cutoff rule picks the smallest set reaching the threshold, so a head with a sharp distribution can reach it with very few keys. A very small selected set can also be fragile to estimation error in the pooled or representative-query scores.
candidates.inference: The paper reports that removing the floor at lower gamma hurts a lot: Llama-3.1-8B at gamma = 0.9 averages 84.78 with no floor and 88.38 with a 1024 floor (Table 10). So the adaptive threshold is not self-sufficient. The floor also bounds the speedup at short context, since 1024 tokens is a large share of a 4k prompt. The link from extreme sparsity to head malfunction is the authors' reported explanation.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: a head puts 0.92 of its estimated mass on a single sink block. At gamma = 0.9, the rule can stop after one block, leaving very little else for the head to attend to.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If gamma is lowered for speed, the results depend on the floor and forced blocks. Changing or removing them, or combining gamma with a different block size or tau, can change accuracy, so gamma cannot be tuned in isolation.
candidates.critical_link: Whether a head still functions at its selected size depends on a floor that is separate from the coverage criterion, and the mass rule does not know about it.
necessary_conditions: Some heads have highly peaked estimated attention so the mass cutoff selects very few keys
Gamma is low enough that those heads' selected sets fall below a functional size
No floor or forced-block rule compensates
defeaters: At high gamma such as 0.95, the paper says the floor is unnecessary because most important tokens are captured; Table 10 shows 89.42 without it versus 89.18 with it
A larger floor does not help further; 2048 gives similar or lower scores than 1024
Model-dependent effects, since GLM shows the same direction but different magnitudes

Do not infer a general failure of cumulative-mass selection; the claim is about coupling with the auxiliary rules
Do not infer that a larger floor keeps improving accuracy; the paper says it does not
